wokeTrap.explanation: Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights markets itself with the prestige of Emily Bronte's classic novel, gorgeous period costumes, and two of the most bankable stars in Hollywood. The trailer promised sweeping romantic drama on the Yorkshire moors. What it delivers is a sexually provocative, BDSM-infused reimagining that turns Bronte's savage Gothic love story into a vehicle for normalizing explicit sexual deviance, masturbation, and kink culture. The film uses the cultural cachet of classic literature to deliver content that most conservative audiences would walk away from if it were marketed honestly. It's not the most severe trap we've scored, but the gap between what's advertised and what's delivered is real.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Wuthering Heights is a moderate woke trap. The marketing leans heavily on the Bronte brand, period aesthetics, and star power to attract a broad audience. What's actually on screen is Emerald Fennell's sexual fever dream: BDSM encounters in the barn, masturbation on the moors, explicit sexual affairs, and a relationship between Heathcliff and Isabella that reframes what Bronte wrote as domestic abuse into consensual kink. The 'classic novel adaptation' packaging conceals content that is aggressively sexualized and ideologically loaded with modern sexual permissiveness. It's not as calculated as Conclave's bait-and-switch, but the mismatch between marketing and content is clear. Conservative parents who assumed 'Bronte adaptation' meant 'safe period drama' are in for a very unpleasant surprise.

summary.overall:
Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights arrives wrapped in the prestige of Emily Bronte's immortal 1847 novel. Don't be fooled. This is not your English teacher's Wuthering Heights. It is not even close to your mother's Wuthering Heights. What Fennell has made is a $80 million art-house provocation that strips Bronte's savage, complex Gothic masterpiece down to its most carnal impulses and then cranks the dial to eleven.

The film opens with a man being publicly hanged. During the hanging, he gets a visible erection. The townspeople, including Catherine Earnshaw, respond with what the screenplay calls 'ecstatic frenzy.' From there, we're off to the races. This is a film that includes masturbation on the moors, BDSM encounters in the barn, explicit sexual affairs, a character treated like a dog as part of a consensual kink arrangement, and enough bodily fluid to fill the Earnshaw estate's well.

Let's be clear about one thing: none of this is in Bronte's novel. Bronte's Wuthering Heights is a story about obsessive love that destroys everyone it touches. It is dark, yes. Violent, sometimes. But it is not an erotic film. Fennell has taken the skeleton of Bronte's plot and dressed it in her own fixations: sexual power, female desire, BDSM dynamics, and the aestheticization of suffering as pleasure.

> SPOILER ALERT: This review discusses major plot points and specific scenes in detail. If you want to remain unspoiled, read only the trope audit section.

---

## The Plot, Fennell Style

The broad strokes are recognizable. Mr. Earnshaw (Martin Clunes), an abrasive alcoholic, brings home a boy from the Liverpool streets to be Cathy's 'pet.' Cathy (Margot Robbie) and Heathcliff (Jacob Elordi) grow up inseparable. Cathy marries the wealthy Edgar Linton (Shazad Latif) for social advancement while loving Heathcliff. Heathcliff overhears her say marrying him would 'degrade' her, and leaves. He returns years later rich and vengeful. Tragedy follows.

But the details have been transformed beyond recognition.

Cathy sees the servants Joseph and Zillah having a BDSM encounter in the barn. She later goes to the moors and masturbates. Heathcliff finds her. They have a 'passionate moment.' When Heathcliff returns rich, he begins a sexual affair with the married Cathy. He also enters a 'loveless, BDSM relationship' with Isabella Linton (Alison Oliver), who, in Fennell's telling, fully understands and consents to being degraded, treated like a dog, and humiliated. In Bronte's novel, Isabella's treatment by Heathcliff is unambiguously abusive. In Fennell's film, it is reframed as kink.

This is the single most ideologically loaded change in the adaptation. Bronte wrote Isabella as a victim of Heathcliff's cruelty. Fennell turns her into a willing participant in her own degradation. The Guardian's review correctly identifies this as grotesque: 'By portraying the young woman Heathcliff abuses as a sexily willing participant in her own degradation, Fennell's adaptation betrays the book, and her audience.'

Cathy eventually starves herself, miscarries, and dies of sepsis. Heathcliff arrives too late. He begs her dead body to haunt him. The end.

---

## What the Film Is Actually Doing

Fennell has stated that her Wuthering Heights is a personal interpretation, not a faithful adaptation. The quotation marks around the title are meant to signal this. Fair enough. But what she's actually created is a film that does three things conservative audiences should understand:

**1. It normalizes BDSM and sexual deviance as romantic.** The film's treatment of the Heathcliff-Isabella relationship is not a cautionary tale. It is presented with aesthetic relish. Isabella consents. She enjoys it. The audience is meant to find this dynamic transgressive and exciting, not abusive and degrading. This is a direct import of modern sex-positive ideology into a period setting, using the cultural authority of Bronte to make it seem timeless rather than contemporary.

**2. It reduces female sexuality to male spectacle.** For a filmmaker who calls herself a feminist, Fennell's camera is remarkably focused on female bodies as objects of desire. Cathy masturbating on the moors is filmed for the audience's consumption. Her body is the terrain the camera explores. Fennell's feminism is the kind that equates sexual display with empowerment, a move that conservative and many traditional feminist critics have long rejected.

**3. It erases the racial politics of the novel.** Bronte's Heathcliff is described as 'dark-skinned,' resembling a 'Lascar' or 'gipsy.' He is racially othered in the text, and that otherness is central to his social exclusion, his rage, and his revenge. By casting the white, Australian Jacob Elordi, Fennell strips this dimension entirely. The New York Times called it 'whitewashing.' Meanwhile, Hong Chau (Vietnamese-American) plays Nelly Dean, reimagined as a lord's illegitimate daughter. The film selectively applies modern racial casting where it serves Fennell's purposes and ignores it where it would create uncomfortable conversations.

### Director: Emerald Fennell

Fennell's filmography tells you everything you need to know.

**Promising Young Woman (2020):** Revenge thriller about a woman targeting men complicit in sexual assault culture. Won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay. Explicitly feminist, explicitly political. The film argues that institutional indifference to sexual violence makes all men complicit. Conservative critics noted the film's black-and-white moral universe.

**Saltburn (2023):** A class satire about a working-class Oxford student who infiltrates a wealthy family's country estate. Featured explicit scenes of homosexual desire, bathtub oral sex, and a character humping a grave. The class commentary was surface-level. The shock was the point. Fennell described it as a 'feminist film' and said she was drawn to making audiences squirm.

**Wuthering Heights (2026):** Takes Bronte's novel and injects BDSM, masturbation, sexual fetishism, and anachronistic sexuality throughout. The pattern is clear and accelerating: each film is more sexually provocative than the last, while Fennell's engagement with actual ideas gets shallower.

### Writer: Emerald Fennell

Same person. Sole writing credit. The screenplay adds material that has no basis in the novel, including the opening hanging/erection scene, the masturbation scene, the BDSM barn encounter, and the reconceiving of Isabella's abuse as consensual kink.

### Producers: LuckyChap Entertainment (Margot Robbie)

LuckyChap is Robbie's production banner. Previous credits include Barbie (2023), which VirtueVigil scored as a Woke Trap, along with both of Fennell's prior films. The company's track record is consistent: mainstream star vehicles with embedded progressive ideology.

### Composer: Anthony Willis (Score), Charli XCX (Songs)

Willis previously scored Saltburn. Charli XCX contributed an entire album of original songs, further anchoring the film in contemporary pop culture rather than period authenticity. The music is anachronistic by design.

### Fidelity Casting Analysis

**Heathcliff (Jacob Elordi):** The single most controversial casting decision. Bronte describes Heathcliff as resembling a 'dark-skinned gipsy' or 'Lascar,' and his racial otherness is central to the character's social exclusion and rage. Casting a tall, white Australian actor erases this dimension. The 2011 Andrea Arnold adaptation correctly cast a Black actor (James Howson). Fennell chose spectacle over fidelity. **Fidelity Score: Low.**

**Catherine Earnshaw (Margot Robbie):** Robbie is 35 playing a character who is 19 in the novel. She's a capable actress but the age discrepancy is noticeable. **Fidelity Score: Moderate.**

**Nelly Dean (Hong Chau):** Reimagined as 'a lord's illegitimate daughter,' making Nelly biracial in a story set in 18th-century Yorkshire. Color-conscious casting that adds a racial element not present in the source. **Fidelity Score: Low.**

---

## Adult Viewer Insight

If you go in expecting a faithful Bronte adaptation, you will be blindsided. This is Emerald Fennell's sexual fantasy wearing Bronte's clothes.

The film is well-crafted on a technical level. The Yorkshire Dales photography is stunning. Elordi and Robbie are physically committed. But the content is something entirely different from what the marketing suggests.

Conservative adults who choose to engage with this film should know: the BDSM content is not incidental. It is the film's thesis. Fennell's argument, across three films now, is that sexual transgression is liberation. That's not subtext. It's the text. Every scene of deviance is filmed with aesthetic relish and narrative endorsement.

The rewriting of Isabella from abuse victim to willing kink participant is the clearest ideological intervention. It reflects the modern sex-positive movement's insistence that BDSM dynamics are inherently valid as long as consent is present, a position that directly contradicts traditional moral teaching about the dignity of the human person in sexual relationships.

Watch it prepared, or skip it entirely. What you cannot do is watch it passively.

---

## Parental Guidance

**Not appropriate for anyone under 18. Hard R-rated content.**

- **Sexual Content:** Severe. Masturbation depicted on screen, BDSM encounters (including a woman treated like a dog), explicit sexual affairs, nudity, and a public hanging with a visible erection in the opening scene.
- **Violence:** Moderate. A brutal whipping scene, a woman kicking a corpse, starvation and death from sepsis.
- **Language:** Mild to moderate period language.
- **Themes:** Obsessive love, betrayal, class exploitation, sexual deviance, abuse reframed as consent.
- **The Specific Concern for Conservative Families:** This film will be marketed as a prestige literary adaptation. High school English teachers may recommend it. Teenagers who have read or are reading Wuthering Heights may seek it out. The content is starkly different from anything in the novel. The sexual material is graphic and ideologically loaded. Do not let the 'Bronte adaptation' label lower your guard.

**Age recommendation:** Adults 18+ only. This is a hard R that earned its rating.

tropeAudit.name: BDSM/kink normalized as consensual romance (Isabella Linton rewrite)
tropeAudit.description: In Bronte's novel, Heathcliff's treatment of Isabella is unambiguous abuse: he degrades, isolates, and brutalizes her. Fennell rewrites Isabella as a willing participant who 'understands the terms of the relationship and consents.' She is treated like a dog, to her 'delight.' This transforms domestic abuse into consensual kink, importing modern BDSM culture directly into the period text. The Guardian called it 'grotesque.' It reflects the sex-positive movement's ideological position that any sexual dynamic is valid under consent, erasing the traditional moral framework that recognizes inherent degradation regardless of stated willingness.

tropeAudit.name: Explicit female sexuality presented as empowerment
tropeAudit.description: Cathy masturbates on the moors. She conducts an explicit affair with Heathcliff while married. These scenes are filmed with aesthetic relish and narrative endorsement, not as moral failings but as expressions of authentic female desire. Fennell has described her work as feminist, and the pattern across her three films is consistent: female sexual agency equals liberation. This is the sex-positive feminist playbook applied to period drama, using Bronte's cultural authority to make contemporary ideology seem timeless.

tropeAudit.name: Color-blind casting selectively applied (Nelly Dean as biracial)
tropeAudit.description: Hong Chau, a Vietnamese-American actress, plays Nelly Dean, reimagined as 'a lord's illegitimate daughter.' This makes Nelly biracial in 18th-century Yorkshire. While color-blind casting is common in period film, the selective application is worth flagging: Fennell applies it for Nelly but erases Heathcliff's canonical racial otherness by casting a white actor.

tropeAudit.name: Whitewashing of racially ambiguous source character (Heathcliff)
tropeAudit.description: Bronte's Heathcliff is described as resembling a 'dark-skinned gipsy' or 'Lascar.' His racial otherness is integral to his social exclusion, his class rage, and his desire for revenge against a white English gentry that rejected him. Casting Jacob Elordi, a white Australian, erases this dimension entirely and reduces Heathcliff's outsider status to mere class. The NYT called it whitewashing. Even by modern progressive standards, this is a regressive casting choice, and Fennell's defense ('he looked like the illustration') was widely mocked.

tropeAudit.name: Feminist framing of shock content as liberation
tropeAudit.description: Fennell has stated she considers all her work feminist. The film's sexual content is not presented as transgression to be morally evaluated. It is presented as the authentic, liberated expression of desire that Victorian and contemporary moral codes suppress. The opening hanging/erection/crowd frenzy sequence sets the film's thesis: human sexuality is primal, bodily, and beyond moral judgment. This is a consistent philosophical position across Fennell's filmography, and it is diametrically opposed to traditional moral teaching on sexual ethics.

tropeAudit.name: Public execution fetishized with sexual arousal
tropeAudit.description: The film opens with a public hanging in which the executed man's visible erection sends spectators into sexual frenzy. While death erections are a documented physiological phenomenon, the scene is not played for historical accuracy. It is played for shock and to establish the film's thesis that sexuality and death are intertwined primal forces beyond moral control. It sets the tone for everything that follows.

tropeAudit.name: Source material desecrated for modern sexual ideology
tropeAudit.description: Fennell's adaptation takes such extreme liberties with the source material that even sympathetic critics describe it as 'very loosely based' on Bronte. The additions are not in service of the novel's themes. They are in service of Fennell's own fixations on sexual transgression, power, and desire. The 'quotation marks around the title' defense does not change the fact that Bronte's name is being used to market content that contradicts the novel's moral and emotional architecture.

tropeAudit.name: Period setting and Yorkshire moors filmed with genuine beauty
tropeAudit.description: Linus Sandgren's 35mm VistaVision cinematography of the Yorkshire Dales is genuinely stunning. The moors, the valleys, the windswept Gothic architecture are captured with a reverence that the narrative doesn't always share. The visual beauty of the scenery is the film's most traditionally grounded element.

tropeAudit.name: Obsessive love shown as destructive and self-annihilating
tropeAudit.description: For all its sexual provocation, the film does not shy away from the destructive consequences of Cathy and Heathcliff's obsession. Cathy starves herself, miscarries, and dies of sepsis. Heathcliff is left to beg a corpse to haunt him. The fundamental Bronte message that all-consuming passion destroys everything in its path does survive Fennell's adaptation, even if it is buried under layers of sexual content.

tropeAudit.name: Cathy's death as tragic consequence of vanity and betrayal
tropeAudit.description: Cathy's decision to marry Edgar for status while loving Heathcliff is presented as a tragic moral failure that leads directly to her destruction. The film does not excuse her choices. She dies as a consequence of her own vanity and Nelly's betrayal. This is a traditionally moral arc, even within Fennell's provocative framework.
